newsitem.title: UK: Rights groups slams Egypt for official censorship.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups slams Egypt for official censorship.

text.p: An international human rights group has strongly condemned the Egyptian government for stifling free speech.
A report issued on Wednesday by the group Article 19 said Egypt had become a religious battleground where advocates of free speech were compelled to exercise self-censorship.

"The Egyptian government is shooting itself in the foot as it cracks down on the peaceful expression of ideas and allows religious institutions to interfere with and censor cultural expression," it said in a statement.

The organisation said a recent suicide attempt by Alaa Hamed, an author known as the Salman Rushdie of Egypt for his troubles with authorities over his writing, underlined the struggle between official censorship and free expression.

Hamed, who is serving a one-year prison sentence for writing a book that prosecutors said was blasphemous and sexually explicit, told Reuters last week that tried to kill himself in a Cairo court to protest against poor prison conditions.

Salman Rushdie is a British writer whose book "The Satanic Verses" was bitterly attacked as blasphemous by the late Iranian spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who issued a death edict against him in 1989.

Intellectuals in Egypt say they are under fire from Moslem militants who want to change Egypt to fit their vision of a strict Islamic state and from the court system, which Islamists have used successfully to curb freedom of expression.
